Health problems of any kind were about as common too: 39 against 41 in 100, and 46 against 46.

Against counselling only or no help, the evidence is weaker. Serious problems: 3 in 100 in both groups (18 trials, 5,032 people; 10 of the trials recorded none). Health problems of any kind: 52 in 100 with a vape against 43, though it could be no real difference.

Some trials found more throat or mouth irritation, cough or dry mouth with vapes; others found fewer breathing symptoms. One found more nausea with patches, gum or similar. how: The study followed about 24,000 US adults for up to 4 years. New heart disease or stroke was reported by 41 of 822 who only vaped, 764 of 14,832 who used neither, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both. The groups differed in age and time followed, so these counts aren't rates.

Allowing for age, health and past smoking, people who only vaped didn't clearly differ from people who used neither. Those who smoked, or smoked and vaped, had about 1.5 times the rate. But the group who used neither included people who had quit smoking, and those who only vaped had smoked more in the past.

In the same study, new lung conditions such as asthma or COPD came to about 2.6 in 100 people a year among those who had ever vaped, against 2.0 among those who never had. Most who vaped had smoked, and without allowing for past smoking the gap looked far bigger. The authors say this can't show that vaping caused it.

Three reviews were done for the US, UK and Australian governments. They found no evidence, or too little, on heart attack, stroke, long-term lung disease or cancer from vaping. The Australian one judged that vapes did cause a lung injury outbreak (EVALI), mostly vapes with THC.

how: A US survey in 2013 and 2014 compared 156 adults who only vaped daily with 3,430 who only smoked daily. Fewer who vaped said they had strong cravings (73 against 87 in 100) or found it hard to go without where it was banned (6 against 29 in 100).

They also waited longer after waking to first use it: about 29 minutes against 20, on average. The question about places where it's banned fits vaping less well. And there's no agreed way to compare the two.

Other US surveys pointed the same way, and so did surveys of young people in England in 2021. There, about half of 16- to 19-year-olds who vaped felt a little or very dependent, against 83 in 100 who smoked. A US expert panel judged that vaping can lead to signs of dependence, and, less firmly, that the risk is lower than with smoking. how: A review pooled 19 small trials in adults who smoke. They hadn't smoked for at least 2 hours, weren't using patches, gum or similar, and mostly weren't trying to quit. They did a short bout of exercise, mostly walking or cycling at a moderate pace, or sat quietly instead.

Right afterwards, people rated their urge to smoke about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale. Every trial pointed the same way, but the size ranged from a fraction of a point to more than 4. The three trials with muscle-tensing exercise showed among the smallest effects.
The urge was rated only once, right after or 5 minutes later. So these trials can't say how long the drop lasts, or whether it helps people stop or stay stopped.

People knew whether they had exercised, and the review didn't check how well the trials were run. 17 of the 19 trials list at least one of the review's authors. The review used its own institutions' money, and its authors report no tobacco or drug-company ties.
